title: The Collapse at Mann Gulch
text:
On August 5, 1949, a crew of fifteen smokejumpers parachuted near a fire in Mann Gulch, in the mountains of Montana. They expected a routine fire they could contain by morning. Joined by a fire guard already on the ground, they followed their foreman, Wagner Dodge, down the gulch. Then the fire jumped across and raced uphill toward them through dry grass.

Dodge ordered the men to turn back and drop their heavy tools. With the fire gaining, he did something no one had seen before: he lit a fire in front of himself, let it burn a patch of grass, and lay down in the ashes. He called the others to join him. None did. Two men reached a gap in the ridge and survived. Dodge survived in his burned patch. Thirteen men died.

In 1993, organizational theorist Karl Weick reanalyzed the disaster, drawing on Norman Maclean's book Young Men and Fire. He argued that the crew suffered a collapse of sensemaking. Their picture of a small, routine fire fell apart, and with it their sense of who led and what each person's role was. Many of the men barely knew each other or Dodge. When the leader's strange order came, the group had no shared structure to hold it together.
lesson: Teams hold together through shared roles and a shared picture of what is happening. Build those in calm times, so that an odd but correct order can still be followed in a crisis.
people: Karl Weick; Wagner Dodge and the Mann Gulch crew
source: Weick, K. E. (1993). The collapse of sensemaking in organizations: The Mann Gulch disaster. Administrative Science Quarterly, 38(4), 628-652.
